source_text: Scimus ex dominico praecepto, quod caro infirma sit, spiritus promptus. Non ergo nobis blandiamur, quia dominus consensit carnem infirmam esse. Propterea enim praedixit spiritum promptum, ut ostenderet, quid cui debeat esse subiectum, scilicet ut caro serviat spiritui, infirmior fortiori, ut ab eo etiam ipsa fortitudinem assumat. Colloquatur spiritus cum carne de communi salute, nec iam de incommodis carceris, sed ipso agone et proelio cogitans. Timebit forsitan caro gladium gravem et crucem excelsam et rabiem bestiarum et summam ignium poenam et omne carnificis ingenium in tormentis, sed spiritus contraponat sibi et carni acerba licet ista, a multis tamen aequo animo excepta, immo et ultro appetita, famae et gloriae causa nec a viris tantum, sed etiam a feminis, ut vos quoque, benedictae, sexui vestro respondeatis. Longum est, si enumerem singulos, qui se gladio confecerint animo suo ducti. De feminis ad manum est. Lucretia, quae vim stupri passa est, cultrum sibi adegit in conspectu propinquorum, ut gloriam castitati suae pareret. Mucius manum suam dexteram in ara cremavit, ut hoc factum eius fama haberet. Minus fecerunt philosophi Heraclitus, qui se bubulo stercore oblitum exussit, item Empedocles, qui in ignes Aetnaei montis desilivit, et Peregrinus, qui non olim se rogo immisit, cum feminae quoque contempserint ignes Dido, cum post virum dilectissimum nubere cogeretur, item Asdrubalis uxor, quae iam ardente Carthagine, ne maritum suum supplicem Scipionis videret, cum filiis suis in incendium patriae devolavit. Regulus, dux Romanorum, captus a Carthaginiensibus, cum se unum pro multis captivis Carthaginiensibus compensari noluisset, maluit hostibus reddi et in arcae genus stipatus undique extrinsecus clavis transfixus tot cruces sensit. Bestias femina libens appetiit, et utique horridiores aspides serpentes tauro vel urso, quas Cleopatra immisit sibi, ne in manus inimici perveniret. Sed mortis metus non tantus est, quantus tormentorum. Itaque cessit carnifici meretrix Atheniensis, quae conscia coniurationis cum propterea torqueretur a tyranno, et non prodidit coniuratos et novissime linguam suam commestam in faciem tyran(??)i expuit, ut nihil agere in se sciret tormenta, etsi ultra perseverarent. Nam quod hodie apud Lacedaemonas sollemnitas maxima est διαμαστίγι(??)σις, id est flagellatio, non latet. In quo sacro ante aram nobiles quique adulescentes flagellis affliguntur, astantibus parentibus et propinquis et, uti perseverent, adhertantibus. Ornamentum enim et gloria deputabitur maiore quidem titulo, si anima potius cesserit plagis, quam corpus. Igitur si tantum terrenae gloriae licet de corporis et animi vigore, ut gladium, ignem, crucem, bestias, tormenta contemnat sub praemio laudis hum(??)ae, possum dicere, modicae sunt istae passiones ad consecutionem gloriae caelestis et divinae mercedis. Tanti vitreum, quanti verum margaritum? Quis ergo non libentissime tantum pro vero habeat erogare, quantum alii pro falso?
thought_title: The spirit must strengthen the flesh for the contest
orientation: Tertullian is addressing the imprisoned Christians, urging them to let the spirit strengthen the flesh by considering examples of pagans who endured suffering for earthly glory.
pass_a_gloss: We know from the Lord's command that the flesh is weak, the spirit is ready. Therefore let us not flatter ourselves, because the Lord agreed that the flesh is weak. For he said beforehand that the spirit is ready for this reason, so that he might show what ought to be subject to what, namely that the flesh should serve the spirit, the weaker to the stronger, so that from it the flesh itself may also take strength. Let the spirit converse with the flesh about their common salvation, thinking no longer about the discomforts of the prison, but about the contest itself and the battle. Perhaps the flesh will fear the heavy sword and the lofty cross and the rage of the beasts and the extreme punishment of the fires and every ingenuity of the executioner in tortures, but let the spirit set against itself and the flesh that these things, though bitter, have been received by many with an even mind, and even sought voluntarily, for the sake of fame and glory, and not only by men, but also by women, so that you too, blessed women, may answer to your sex. It would be long if I should enumerate one by one those who have killed themselves with the sword, led by their own mind. Of women it is at hand. Lucretia, who suffered the violence of rape, drove a knife into herself in the sight of her relatives, so that she might produce glory for her chastity. Mucius burned his own right hand on the altar, so that his deed might have fame. The philosophers did less: Heraclitus, who smeared himself with cow dung and burned himself up, likewise Empedocles, who leaped down into the fires of Mount Etna, and Peregrinus, who not long ago sent himself onto a pyre, since women too have despised fires: Dido, when after her most beloved husband she was being forced to marry, likewise the wife of Hasdrubal, who, when Carthage was already burning, so that she might not see her husband as a suppliant of Scipio, flew down with her sons into the fire of her fatherland. Regulus, a leader of the Romans, captured by the Carthaginians, when he had refused that he alone be exchanged for many Carthaginian captives, preferred to be handed back to the enemy and, packed into a kind of box, pierced on every side from the outside with nails, felt as many crosses. A woman willingly sought beasts, and indeed serpents more horrible than a bull or bear, which Cleopatra sent upon herself, so that she might not come into the hands of the enemy. But the fear of death is not as great as the fear of tortures. And so the Athenian courtesan yielded to the executioner, who, aware of the conspiracy, when she was being tortured for that reason by the tyrant, both did not betray the conspirators and finally spat out her own tongue, chewed up, into the face of the tyrant, so that the tortures might know that they could accomplish nothing against her, even if they should persist further. For what is today among the Lacedaemonians the greatest solemnity, the diamastigosis, that is, flagellation, is not hidden. In which sacred rite before the altar all the noble youths are afflicted with whips, while their parents and relatives stand by and urge them to persevere. For it will be reckoned an ornament and glory, with a greater title indeed, if the soul rather than the body should yield to the blows. Therefore if so much is permitted to earthly glory from the vigor of body and mind, that it despises sword, fire, cross, beasts, tortures under the reward of human praise, I can say that these sufferings are moderate for the attainment of heavenly glory and divine reward. How much is a glass pearl worth, how much a true pearl? Who therefore would not most willingly spend as much for the true as others spend for the false?

choices.english: the flesh is weak, the spirit is ready
choices.why: Echoes Matthew 26:41; 'ready' preserves the sense of eagerness/willingness in promptus, distinct from 'willing' which would blur the contrast with infirmus
rejected: the flesh is weak, the spirit is willing

choices.why: Glossary term for the martyrdom contest, keeping the athletic metaphor
Glossary term; used for both earthly and heavenly glory, preserving the contrast Tertullian draws
Direct address to the female martyrs; 'blessed' preserves the vocative force and the honorific tone
Glossary term for voluntary pursuit of suffering out of vanity; appears in the following section but the concept is anticipated here
Modicus means 'moderate, small in measure'; Tertullian is arguing that Christian sufferings are small compared to the reward

pass_b_english: We know from the Lord's command that the flesh is weak, the spirit is ready (Matthew 26:41). So let us not flatter ourselves because the Lord agreed that the flesh is weak. He said the spirit is ready precisely to show what should be subject to what: the flesh should serve the spirit, the weaker serving the stronger, so that from it the flesh may also take strength. Let the spirit converse with the flesh about their common salvation, thinking no longer of the prison's discomforts but of the contest itself and the battle. The flesh will perhaps fear the heavy sword, the towering cross, the rage of beasts, the extreme punishment of fire, and every device the executioner's ingenuity can bring to torture. But let the spirit set before itself and the flesh that, bitter as these things are, many have accepted them with equanimity—indeed, have even sought them out voluntarily—for the sake of reputation and glory, and not only men but women too, so that you also, blessed women, may answer to your sex. It would take long to list one by one those who have killed themselves with the sword, driven by their own resolve. Among women, an example is close at hand. Lucretia, who suffered the violence of rape, drove a knife into herself in the sight of her relatives, to produce glory for her chastity. Mucius burned his own right hand on the altar, so that his deed might win renown. The philosophers did less: Heraclitus, who smeared himself with cow dung and burned to death; likewise Empedocles, who leaped into the fires of Mount Etna; and Peregrinus, who not long ago threw himself onto a pyre. Women too have despised fire: Dido, when she was forced to marry after the death of her most beloved husband; likewise Hasdrubal's wife, who, when Carthage was already burning, threw herself with her children into the flames of her homeland rather than see her husband begging Scipio. Regulus, a Roman leader, was captured by the Carthaginians. When he refused to be exchanged one man for many Carthaginian captives, he preferred to be handed back to the enemy, and packed into a kind of box pierced on every side from the outside with nails, he felt as many crosses. A woman willingly sought out beasts—and serpents more terrible than a bull or bear—which Cleopatra applied to herself, to avoid falling into the hands of her enemy. But the fear of death is not so great as the fear of torture. So the Athenian courtesan yielded to the executioner: she was party to a conspiracy, and when she was tortured by the tyrant for that reason, she did not betray the conspirators, and finally bit off her own tongue and spat it into the tyrant's face, so that the torturers might know they could accomplish nothing against her, even if they continued. For what is today the greatest solemnity among the Lacedaemonians—the diamastigosis, that is, the whipping—is no secret. In that sacred rite, noble young men are beaten with whips before the altar, while their parents and relatives stand by and urge them to persevere. It is counted as an ornament and glory, and with a greater title, if the spirit rather than the body yields to the blows. Therefore, if so much is permitted to earthly glory from the vigor of body and spirit that it despises sword, fire, cross, beasts, and torture under the reward of human praise, I can say these sufferings are moderate for obtaining heavenly glory and divine reward. How much is a glass pearl worth, compared to a true one? Who then would not most gladly spend as much for the true as others spend for the false?

last_rejected.quote: so that the tortures might know they could accomplish nothing against her
last_rejected.source_quote: ut nihil agere in se sciret tormenta
last_rejected.why: Subject is the tyrant, not the tortures; 'sciret' governs 'nihil agere': so the tyrant would know tortures accomplish nothing in her.
last_rejected.fix: so that the tyrant might know the tortures accomplished nothing in her, even if they continued
last_rejected.ruling: Latin has subject 'tormenta' with verb 'sciret', meaning 'so the tortures might know they could do nothing to her'.
